 Election Workers Braced for Chaos. They Got a Smooth Election Day. 
 Governing talked with election officials across the country on Wednesday about what went right and how they handled the few problems that arose.
 Nov. 4, 2026 •  
 Jule Pattison-Gordon 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Twitter 
 Email 
 Print 
 Voters fill out their ballots at Ypsilanti Township's 4th precinct at the Washtenaw Golf Club, Tues., Nov. 3, 2026. (Chad Livengood/TNS) 
 By Jule Pattison-Gordon.
 In Brief: 
 Fears of federal interference didn’t come to pass. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn’t show, and only a few localities reported questionable behavior by Department of Justice monitors.
 Election officials kept voting going, despite flooding and power outages in some areas.
 Contra Costa County, Calif., had to fix a ballot issue, and Broward County, Fla., had a delayed start.
Despite fears about possible federal interference at polling places, election security and voter confidence in results, Tuesday night’s elections largely ran smoothly, eight election officials told Governing on Wednesday .  
“We didn't have any surprises, and I hate to jinx myself, but that was a boring election, and we loved it,” says Tonya Wichman, director of elections for Defiance County, Ohio. In her more than 11 years on the job, “it was probably the smoothest election we've had.”
Election officials prepared heavily, and while individual jurisdictions across the U.S. faced issues ranging from power outages to bomb threats to technical glitches, election officials were quick to respond and ensure voting could continue.
The relatively uneventful night — at least from an administrative perspective — was a welcome relief for election administrators, who have faced a stressful election cycle. The White House has been exceptionally hostile toward election officials in public statements, and the president has appeared eager to sow doubt about the trustworthiness of election results.   His attempts to prevent certification of Alaska's results should the incumbent lose and to have California set aside 20,000 ballots on charges they could be from noncitizens failed in the courts.
Officials have had to grapple with this political firestorm even as they face all the usual administrative challenges of running an election, including defending voter information against cyber attacks (ballot machines are not connected to the Internet and are not vulnerable to hacks themselves). Leading up to election day, however, most administrators didn’t seem overly worried.
“People know what they need to do,” Philadelphia City Commissioner Seth Bluestein told Governing in the run-up to the elections. “They’ve run elections before, so they are ready to do the job and get everything across the finish line.”
As the night went on and it became increasingly clear that Democrats would win both chambers and take the governorships even in some solid red states , President Donald Trump appeared uncharacteristically subdued in interviews, telling the New York Times that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results and that he is willing to work with Democrats.
It’s a stark turn for a president who has repeatedly aimed to interfere with how elections are run, including suggesting Republicans “ nationalize ” voting and making a last-minute attempt to overhaul mail-in voting before the Supreme Court stepped in.
This Election Day, the Department of Justice (DOJ) sent a flood of election monitors to every state. Election monitors are a normal part of Election Day and have always been sent out to ensure voting rights laws are being followed. These monitors are not supposed to interfere with voting. But the size of the deployment and the Trump administration’s repeated efforts to cast doubt on elections made some state officials uneasy . Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold told PBS that the DOJ is "hostile" to free and fair elections and that deploying monitors could be an effort to "lay the groundwork for MAGA and Trump to reject the results if they don't go their way." 
These fears did not come to pass. In many counties, election officials said they saw no sign of election monitors near polling places. That includes Contra Costa County, Calif., where officials had clashed with the federal government over demands for the county to set aside 407 ballots on charges they could be cast by noncitizens. Monitors were in Leon County, Fla., where Supervisor of Elections Mike Earely said they acted appropriately, carrying no weapons and neither attempting to talk to voters nor entering polling sites. Instead, monitors simply checked Spanish-language signage and for compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
A few locations reported questionable behavior. In Bernalillo County , N.M., DOJ monitors were “asking some unusual questions and questioning voters,” a secretary of state’s office spokesperson told ProPublica ; the DOJ promised to “address” the accusations. Monitors in Mecklenburg County, N.C., allegedly asked to see the phones of voters leaving the polls. Monitors in two Michigan cities reportedly asked to see election workers’ training materials, something the DOJ told state officials they aren’t supposed to do.
Some voters and election officials had also feared Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents turning out to the polls thanks to comments from former Trump administration official Steve Bannon, though the administration maintained it would not send immigration enforcement to voting sites. Leon County experienced a false alarm on the first day of early voting, when two U.S. Customs and Border Protection cars were spotted by a polling site; ultimately Supervisor Earley discovered these were just agents driving north out of Florida who had stopped in hoping to vote. In Broward County, Fla., officials saw posts online claiming ICE agents were present at polls but found the claim to be untrue, says Supervisor of Elections Joe Scott.
Among the biggest challenges of the day wasn’t the White House but the weather. Utah Lt. Gov Deidre Henderson issued an emergency declaration to let 5,000 voters in parts of San Juan County vote online after flooding washed out roads. In Leon County, a severe storm knocked out power at some polling places during the last two hours of Election Day; but staff got out flashlights and battery-powered lights. The ballot scanners ran on batteries. The county also was ready with preprinted paper ballots and paper poll books if needed, and teams of election “rovers” ready to drive between sites with extra supplies, including generators. In St. Louis County, Mo., the biggest issue of the day was rain hitting as poll workers were transferring ballots in canvas bags at the end of the day, says Director of Elections Eric Frey. This necessitated drying them out with industrial fans (the incident didn’t affect tabulation, as the county used information on USB sticks from the ballot scanners).
While some jurisdictions had issues with their materials or tools, these appeared to be isolated issues.
In Contra Costa County, 187 voters from a low-income city were miscategorized and sent a ballot that didn’t include five municipal races; the county discovered the issue at 11 a.m. on Election Day, corrected it by noon and tried to alert voters. But any affected voter casting a ballot by mail or before that time had a more limited ballot. If those races are won by a slim margin, the county may have to hold a special election, says Clerk Recorder Kristin Connelly.
In Broward County, the start of polling was delayed by 20 minutes due to a glitch. Recent redistricting meant polling locations now served voters from multiple precincts, and they’d started using a scanning tool, linked to the electronic poll book, to help verify that they were handing out the correct ballot to each voter. This had gone fine during the primaries in August, but on Tuesday a code issue led scanners to falsely flag the ballots as wrong, Scott says. The glitch briefly delayed voting but poll workers quickly switched to manually checking ballots to keep the show running. During the delay, some people in line to vote left the polling place. The county tried to reach out to anyone who complained of the issue on social media to let them know it was now resolved.
Ultimately, workers overcame these issues and the election went off about as smoothly as possible. “It was an extremely successful election day for us,” says Michelle Blue, elections director for Dakota County, Minn.
